evidence: Turner groups Lahnda hekk/hikk, Punjabi ikk/hekka, northwestern akh/yakh, Oriya eka and Gujarati ek/eko in the retained-k ēkka branch. These simple survey numerals, including both Awankari ekʰ/īka alternatives, match that family with regional vowels, aspiration and inflection. Turner leaves emphatic doubling versus early Sanskrit reborrowing unresolved; this link does not resolve that prehistoric alternative.

Turner gives Lahnda nõ and Awankari naɔ̃, Punjabi naũ and the northwestern nasal-vowel series under nava nine. Both Gujari slash alternatives are the same numeral family, with diphthong versus contracted vowel; neither contains an extra classifier.

Turner lists Awankari dā, Oriya dasa and daś throughout Western Pahari under daśa ten. The survey responses match those regional numeral stems, with local vowel, sibilant and aspiration variation; both Awankari alternatives are the same form. The separate dā/das response is excluded because Turner marks Punjabi das as a Hindi loan.

Turner records Oriya sa/sae, Western Pahari śau and Gujarati sɔ in the śata hundred family. These whole survey hundred responses fit the regional weakened-intervocalic-t vowel series; the western h/x onsets are compared with the s/h variation elsewhere in the same Bhili surveys. The mapping is comparative, without claiming that every onset and glide is independently established as a regular sound change.

The complete response is one + hundred: the initial ek matches Turner’s ēkka family, and haū/hõ/ho matches the western śata hundred series (compare Gujarati sɔ, Marathi śẽ and regional h-onset survey forms). The hyphenated and spaced answers are represented with two ordered components; no single ancient compound or source-spelling change is asserted.
